1198.title: The Tanya's two souls
1198.hook: the Tanya describes an animal soul and a godly soul in each person
1198.carry: two souls, one city: let the godly soul lead
1198.howItsDone: In Chabad study, the opening chapters of the Tanya on the animal soul and the godly soul are taught as a map of inner life, used to understand the struggle in prayer and in daily choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tanya, and its in-between person who feels the pull and still chooses. Your line: the in-between person. Today, the voices inside that pull.

The alarm goes off. One voice says: five more minutes, you've earned it. Another says: get up, there's someone you promised to call. You're hungry and someone at the table is hungrier. One voice says take the bigger piece. Another says pass it. An argument like that needs more than one voice in there. Yesterday's book, the Tanya, doesn't treat that as a glitch. It opens by giving the voices names.
screen: `FIVE MORE MINUTES.` → `GET UP, YOU PROMISED.` → `MORE THAN ONE VOICE IN THERE.`

segments.voice: Two souls. The Tanya teaches that each Jew has two souls. First, the animal soul. It's the life of the body: hunger, tiredness, the instinct to protect yourself and get what you need. Animal here isn't an insult. Teachers of the Tanya explain it as the life a person shares with other living creatures. Its center is self: me first, mine, more. Second, the godly soul. The Tanya describes it with a phrase borrowed from the book of Job: a part of God above. Its pull is toward God, toward giving, toward the good beyond itself. Proverbs gives a picture that fits: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." Third, the city. In a later chapter the Tanya compares the body to a small city, and the two souls to two kings, each wanting to rule it. Every thought, every word, every act is a piece of ground one of them wins. That's yesterday's in-between person, seen from the inside: two kings, one city, and a daily choice about who governs. Fourth, the aim. The goal isn't to kill the animal soul. It keeps you alive. The hope, in Chabad teaching, is that the godly soul leads, and that over time even the animal soul's energy, its hunger and drive, can be turned toward good. Remember the lesson on serving through the body: the appetite isn't the enemy. It's the city's other citizen, waiting to be led well.
screen: `THE ANIMAL SOUL: THE LIFE OF THE BODY.` · `THE GODLY SOUL: A PART OF GOD ABOVE.` · `TWO KINGS, ONE SMALL CITY.` · `NOT TO KILL, BUT TO LEAD.` · then, large: `TWO SOULS.`

segments.voice: Listen inside for the animal soul, tired, hungry, wanting this to be over, and without arguing, just hear it: there you are. Then listen for the quieter voice, the one that leans toward someone else, toward the good, toward God if you pray, and hear it too. Sit with both for a while, two voices in one small city; if you pray, you can ask that the quieter one lead.
Two souls. In the Tanya, the animal soul that gives life to the body, and the godly soul, a part of God above, each pulling toward its own. Today's word.
Your line: two souls, one city: let the godly soul lead. Two kings, one small city. I'll be here tomorrow.

1199.title: Rebbe Nachman's circle of joy
1199.hook: Rebbe Nachman taught that being joyful always is a great mitzvah
1199.carry: joy is a mitzvah, kept up on hard days
1199.tomorrow: If you can damage, you can repair
1199.howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim sing and dance as a deliberate practice of joy, and the saying that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always has been set to song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two souls: two kings and one small city. Your line: two souls, one city: let the godly soul lead. Today, a wedding, late at night.
screen: `TWO SOULS, ONE CITY: LET THE GODLY SOUL LEAD.`

segments.voice: A wedding, late at night. The music is loud and a circle of dancers is spinning. Off to the side stands a man who isn't dancing. His face is heavy. Something is wrong in his life, and it shows. Then two of the dancers break the circle, take him by the hands, and pull him in. He resists for a step or two. Then he's turning with them, still carrying whatever he carries, but carried along too. Rebbe Nachman of Breslov used a scene like this to teach about joy. And he made a demand about it that sounds impossible.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF DANCERS.` → `A MAN WITH A HEAVY FACE.` → `PULLED INTO THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Always joyful. Rebbe Nachman taught that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always. First, the word always. In Hebrew it's tamid, the word for the offering that was brought in the Temple without a break, morning and evening. The psalm uses it too: "I have set the LORD always before me." Always isn't a mood. It's a practice that keeps going. Second, it's work. Rebbe Nachman didn't pretend joy comes easily. Breslov teaching passes on his advice that a person should push with all their strength to be glad, and when nothing else works, to do something a little silly, something light, to break the heaviness. Joy, here, is something you make, not something you wait for. Third, the circle. That's the scene from the hook, and it's his. When joy is strong, it doesn't run from sadness. It reaches over, takes sadness by the hands, and pulls it into the dance. The sadness isn't erased. It's brought in, and it starts to move. Fourth, how this differs from a week ago. Simcha, a week ago, opened the heart. Rebbe Nachman adds the hard part: always. On the bad days too. Especially then. Not because pain doesn't matter, but because, for him, a heavy heart is the very place joy is needed most.
screen: `TAMID: WITHOUT A BREAK.` · `JOY IS WORK, NOT WEATHER.` · `JOY PULLS SADNESS INTO THE DANCE.` · `ON THE BAD DAYS TOO.` · then, large: `ALWAYS JOYFUL.`

segments.voice: Let the corners of your mouth lift, even if it feels a little silly; Rebbe Nachman wouldn't mind silly. Breathe in and think of one thing you're glad exists, breathe out and let a little heaviness go, and if something hard is sitting with you today, don't push it away: invite it into the circle. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words, I have set the LORD always before me.
Always joyful. Rebbe Nachman's teaching that being joyful always is a great mitzvah: joy as steady work, pulling sadness into the dance. Today's words.
Your line: joy is a mitzvah, kept up on hard days. Joy, for Rebbe Nachman, is work you keep doing, not weather. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1199 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IF YOU CAN DAMAGE, YOU CAN REPAIR.`

1200.title: If you can damage, you can repair
1200.hook: Rebbe Nachman: if you believe you can damage, believe you can repair
1200.carry: teshuvah: if you can damage, you can repair
1200.howItsDone: In Jewish practice teshuvah, returning, means admitting a wrong, regretting it, making it right with anyone harmed, and resolving to change; Breslov teaching stresses never giving up on that return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebbe Nachman's demand: always joyful, joy pulling sadness into the dance. Your line: joy is a mitzvah, kept up on hard days. Today, a sentence some people say after a bad day.
screen: `JOY IS A MITZVAH, KEPT UP ON HARD DAYS.`

segments.voice: "I ruin everything." Some people say it out loud after a bad day. Some only think it. A sharp word at dinner, a forgotten promise, a friendship that went quiet because you didn't call. The list gets long, and it starts to feel like proof. Here's something odd about that sentence, though. It takes your power very seriously. It believes, completely, that what you do has effects. Rebbe Nachman of Breslov noticed exactly that, and turned it around.
screen: `I RUIN EVERYTHING.` → `THE LIST STARTS TO FEEL LIKE PROOF.` → `IT TAKES YOUR POWER SERIOUSLY.`

segments.voice: You can repair. Rebbe Nachman taught, in words his students wrote down: if you believe that you can damage, then believe that you can repair. First, the logic. It's almost a trick of fairness. You already believe your actions matter, because you believe they did harm. Fine, he says. Then you can't turn around and claim your actions are powerless when it comes to fixing. The same hands. The same power. Second, the old root. This isn't new to Hasidism. The prophet Ezekiel tells the people to cast away their wrongs and "make you a new heart and a new spirit." Make. As if a heart is something a person can work on. That's the heart of teshuvah, returning: the door is open, and you can walk through it. Third, the enemy. For Rebbe Nachman, the great danger after a wrong isn't the wrong itself. It's despair, the conclusion that nothing can be done. Breslov teaching treasures his saying that there is no despair in the world at all. Despair closes the door teshuvah opens. Fourth, the scale. Repair doesn't have to be large. Brought home, the teaching works at the size of an apology, a phone call, a mended chair, a sentence you take back. His teaching doesn't ask for everything to be repaired. It asks for one repair, seen as possible, and then made.
screen: `THE SAME HANDS, THE SAME POWER.` · `MAKE YOU A NEW HEART.` · `THE ENEMY IS DESPAIR.` · `ONE REPAIR AT A TIME.` · then, large: `YOU CAN REPAIR.`

segments.voice: Let one small damage come to mind, something you broke or let slide that you could actually touch today, and look at it without the old sentence, I ruin everything. Instead, say Rebbe Nachman's turn to yourself, if I could damage it, I can repair it, and picture the first step: the text, the fix, the words. If you pray, you can ask for help with the step.
You can repair. Rebbe Nachman's teaching: if you believe you can damage, believe you can repair. The same power that harms can mend. Today's words.
Your line: teshuvah: if you can damage, you can repair. The same hands, the same power. Go gently.

1201.title: The Kotzker and emet
1201.hook: the Kotzker rebbe demanded truth without comfort
1201.carry: emet can't be imitated, only lived
1201.howItsDone: Jewish teaching counts honesty, in speech and in the heart, among the basic demands of the Torah; the sayings of the Kotzker rebbe are retold in Hasidic and wider Jewish circles as a challenge to empty piety.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebbe Nachman's turn: if you believe you can damage, believe you can repair. Your line: teshuvah: if you can damage, you can repair. Today, a colder voice.
screen: `TESHUVAH: IF YOU CAN DAMAGE, YOU CAN REPAIR.`

segments.voice: These last days have been warm ones. Joy that opens. A rebbe at the head of the table. Pulling sadness into the dance. Today the temperature drops. In the small Polish town of Kotzk lived a Hasidic rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel, who had little patience for warmth that wasn't real. Stories about him are sharp, short, and a little frightening. Tradition says he would rather have a handful of followers who were honest than crowds who were comfortable. His whole life circled one word, and he wanted it without any padding.
screen: `THE TEMPERATURE DROPS.` → `A REBBE IN KOTZK.` → `NO PADDING.`

segments.voice: Truth. In Hebrew, emet. First, the Bible's standard. The psalm asks who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and part of its answer is the one who "speaketh truth in his heart." Not only with the mouth. In the heart, where nobody checks. Second, the sages. The Talmud teaches that God's seal is truth. And it notices something about the word itself: emet is spelled with the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a letter from the middle, and the last. Truth, the sages suggest, runs the whole length, beginning to end. Third, the Kotzker. Sayings attributed to him are passed on by his followers, and one of them goes like this: everything in the world can be imitated except truth, because truth that's imitated isn't truth anymore. He aimed it first at religious life. Prayer done for show, piety performed for the neighbors, a warm feeling worn like a coat. To him, those were imitations, and he'd take an honest struggle over a comfortable fake. Fourth, the cost, said fairly. The Kotzker's way is hard, and Hasidic tradition itself remembers him as a fierce and solitary figure. Not every teacher walked his road, and the other Hasidic teachers in these lessons lean toward warmth and joy. His question can sit underneath the warm paths too. Is this real? Am I telling the truth in my heart, where nobody checks? That's what fiercely means here. Not cruelty to others. Honesty with yourself, without padding.
screen: `SPEAKETH TRUTH IN HIS HEART.` · `FIRST, MIDDLE AND LAST.` · `TRUTH CAN'T BE IMITATED.` · `HONEST WITH YOURSELF, NO PADDING.` · then, large: `TRUTH, FIERCELY.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself one plain question, and let the answer come without dressing it up: what am I pretending about? Maybe a feeling you claim not to have, a habit you call fine, a reason that isn't the real one; when it comes, don't argue with it or punish yourself, just let it be true for a minute. If you pray, you can stand before God with exactly that, and nothing extra.
Truth. Emet in Hebrew, God's seal for the sages, and for the Kotzker rebbe the one thing that can't be imitated. Today's word.
Your line: emet can't be imitated, only lived. Not cruelty to others: honesty with yourself. That's today, done.

1202.title: Joseph and the Izbicer's Hidden Will
1202.hook: the Izbicer taught that God's will can hide inside human choices
1202.carry: god's will can hide inside our choices
1202.howItsDone: Students of the Izbicer read Mei HaShiloach slowly, often with a teacher, alongside the weekly Torah portion, and his teachings are discussed in Hasidic and other study circles as a way to think about choice and providence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kotzker rebbe and his demand for truth with no comfort added. Your line: truth, fiercely. Today, a voice that came out of that same fierce room.

Joseph's brothers stand in front of him in Egypt, terrified. Years before, they threw him in a pit and sold him. Now he rules the country's grain, and they need bread. He could punish them. Instead he says something strange: "So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God." They did it, and they remember doing it. And Joseph tells them a second story was running underneath theirs the whole time. One Hasidic teacher pressed that idea into places that still unsettle his readers.
screen: `THE BROTHERS IN EGYPT.` → `IT WAS NOT YOU, BUT GOD.` → `A STORY UNDER THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Hidden will. The teacher is Rabbi Mordechai Yosef Leiner, called the Izbicer after his town, Izbica. Tradition says he learned in the Kotzker's circle before going his own way. His teachings were gathered in a book called Mei HaShiloach, the waters of Shiloah. First, the old line. The Talmud says everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven. Standing in awe of God is your own choice. Second, the Izbicer's push. In his readings, even our choices can carry God's will inside them, hidden. A person acts, sure they're acting alone, and later it turns out something larger was moving through the act. Joseph saw it: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." Third, the hard part. The Izbicer reads some uncomfortable stories this way, people in the Torah who seem to break the rules, and asks whether a deeper will was at work. Readers argue over these passages; some find them daring, some unsettling. Fourth, the guardrail. He did not tell people to drop the commandments and follow their urges. In ordinary life, his readers say, a person walks by the law. The hidden will is something you might glimpse, if at all, looking back. You can't see the whole of your own story from inside it: a wrong turn, a closed door, a person who hurt you. The Izbicer doesn't say the hurt was good. He says the last word on what it meant may not be yours to write yet.
screen: `THE IZBICER AND HIS BOOK.` · `IN THE HANDS OF HEAVEN.` · `GOD'S WILL INSIDE OUR CHOICES.` · `SEEN, IF AT ALL, LOOKING BACK.` · then, large: `HIDDEN WILL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your life you still don't understand, not a crisis, just something that never made sense: a plan that fell apart, a meeting you didn't expect. Hold it gently, without explaining it or calling it good, and on each breath out, loosen your grip on needing the answer today. If you pray, you can hold it there, in the hands of Heaven.
Hidden will. The Izbicer's teaching that God's will can hide inside human choices, seen, if at all, only looking back, while ordinary life still walks by the law. Today's word.
Your line: God's will can hide inside our choices. Some stories can only be read looking back. See you tomorrow.

1203.title: The courts
1203.hook: Hasidic dynasties such as Ger, Belz, Satmar and Bobov are named for towns
1203.howItsDone: Hasidim belong to a particular court and its rebbe, often for generations; they pray in that court's synagogues, sing its melodies and keep its customs, and gather at the rebbe's table on Shabbat and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Izbicer and the hidden will: God's purpose tucked inside human choices, seen, if at all, looking back. Today, the families the Hasidim belong to.

A man in a long black coat steps off a bus in Brooklyn, or in Jerusalem, and someone asks him where he's from. He names a town in Europe he may never have visited. A small place, a dot on a map. He isn't confused about his address. He's telling you which family of Hasidim he belongs to. Hasidic courts often go by neither a founder's name nor an idea, but by a place.
screen: `A COAT, A BUS, A QUESTION.` → `A TOWN HE'S NEVER SEEN.` → `NAMED BY A PLACE.`

segments.voice: The courts. In Yiddish, a hoyf: the court that gathers around a rebbe. First, the names. Ger comes from Góra Kalwaria, a town near Warsaw. Belz is a town in Galicia. Satmar is the Yiddish name for Satu Mare, in Romania. Bobov is Bobowa, in southern Poland. And Lubavitch, the name carried by the court of Shneur Zalman's Chabad line, is a small town too. Each court took its name from the place where its rebbe lived and Hasidim came to him. Second, the dynasty. Earlier in this block you met the rebbe as guide for his followers. When a rebbe dies, a court usually looks for the next one in his family: a son, a son-in-law, a grandson. So the name, the melodies and the customs pass down like an heirloom. Sometimes two heirs each draw followers, and one court becomes two. Third, the move. The Jewish life of these towns was destroyed in the Holocaust. Survivors carried the courts to new homes, in places like Brooklyn, Jerusalem and Bnei Brak. The town is gone from their daily life, but its name still stands over the door. Fourth, what it means for a Hasid. To say I'm a Belzer, or a Bobover, is to say: this is my rebbe, these are my tunes, this is how my family prays and dresses and marks the festivals. Each court has its own feel. None speaks for all Hasidim, and Hasidim don't all agree about each other. It's the old Hebrew sense of a court, a courtyard, a gathering place: "a day in thy courts is better than a thousand."

segments.voice: Say one name from today quietly a few times: Ger, Belz, Satmar, Bobov or Lubavitch. Then think of a place your own family carries in its name or its stories, a town, a street, a country someone left, and what you still do because of it: a food, a word, a habit. Sit with the two places side by side.
The courts. The Hasidic communities gathered around a rebbe, usually passed down within his family, and named for the European towns where they began. Today's word.
Your line: named for towns. A name can carry a whole way of life across an ocean. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1204.title: Why Hasidim Dress This Way
1204.hook: Hasidic dress keeps the memory of old Eastern Europe
1204.carry: dress that remembers, dress to meet god
1204.tomorrow: The Niggun: A Song Without Words
1204.howItsDone: In Hasidic courts, men wear a long dark coat and tie a gartel for prayer, and on Shabbat and festivals married men in some courts put on a fur shtreimel or spodik; the details differ from court to court.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the courts: Ger, Belz, Satmar, Bobov, each one named for towns its Hasidim may never have seen. Today, what those Hasidim wear.

A closet holds a story if you know how to read it. A wedding dress in a garment bag. A grandfather's watch in a drawer. A jersey that only comes out on game day. On a Friday afternoon in a Hasidic neighborhood, the men come out in long black silk coats, and some wear round fur hats, wide and tall, that look like nothing else on the street. To a passerby it looks like a costume. To the people wearing it, it's closer to that watch in the drawer.
screen: `A CLOSET HOLDS A STORY.` → `FRIDAY AFTERNOON.` → `NOT A COSTUME.`

segments.voice: Clothes remember. First, the pieces. The long coat, called a bekishe or a kapote. The fur hat on Shabbat, a shtreimel, or in some courts a taller one, a spodik. A belt, the gartel, tied around the waist for prayer. Each court has its own details, down to the shape of a hat. Second, the memory. Tradition says this is, broadly, how Jewish men and nobles in parts of Eastern Europe once dressed. The world around them changed its clothes. The Hasidim kept theirs. So the coat says: we have not forgotten where we come from. A midrash some Hasidim quote says that in Egypt the Israelites held on to their own names and their own language, and some versions add their own dress. Third, dressing for God. The Talmud tells of a sage who would put on fine shoes before praying, citing the prophet Amos: "prepare to meet thy God, O Israel." Hasidim speak of the gartel in the same spirit, a line drawn around the body before standing to pray. Fourth, what it isn't. The clothes are not the faith, and Hasidim themselves don't say they are. Other Jews dress in all kinds of ways and pray just as seriously. But cloth can hold a memory the way a melody can. Look back over this week: two souls, always joyful, you can repair, truth, fiercely, hidden will, named for towns. And today, a coat that remembers.
screen: `BEKISHE, SHTREIMEL, GARTEL.` · `THE WORLD CHANGED; THEY DIDN'T.` · `PREPARE TO MEET THY GOD.` · `CLOTH HOLDS A MEMORY.` · then, large: `CLOTHES REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Look down at what you're wearing right now and pick one thing: a ring, a scarf, a pair of shoes. Ask where it came from, who gave it, where you bought it, what you were doing the first time you wore it, and let the memory come up. Then picture one thing you might put on for a reason you can name: to honor someone, or to get ready for something that matters.
Clothes remember. Hasidic dress, the long coat, the fur hat, the prayer belt, keeps the memory of old Eastern Europe and turns getting dressed into getting ready. Today's word.
Your line: dress that remembers, dress to meet God. The coat keeps a memory; the gartel gets you ready to pray. Until tomorrow.
